paragraphs.text: In the thin-lens, paraxial model used here, the focal positions determine the imaging properties of a lens.
Knowing the source-to-lens distance and focal length lets us locate the image without tracing the path inside the lens or drawing the exact shapes of its two spherical surfaces.
We can therefore represent a converging lens by the symbol in Figure 177 and a diverging lens by the symbol in Figure 178.
Within this approximation, **rays from the same object point correspond to the same image point after passing through the lens**.

A real image point is an intersection of actual refracted rays;
a virtual image point is an intersection of backward extensions of diverging rays.

Imaging each object point produces an image of the whole object;
this does not assert exact concurrence for arbitrary ray angles or apertures.
When the foci and optical center of a converging lens are known, three special rays are convenient for constructing an image.
A ray incident parallel to the principal axis refracts through the focus on the other side of the lens.
A ray passing through the object-side focus before reaching the lens emerges parallel to the principal axis, by reversibility of the light path.

A ray through the optical center keeps its direction;
its small translation in a real lens is neglected in the thin-lens approximation.
The last rule does not claim that translation inside a real lens is exactly zero.
Figure 179 shows how to construct the image of the object $AB$.

First locate the image of $A$: send $AC$ parallel to the principal axis so that it refracts through the far focus, and send $AD$ through the object-side focus so that it emerges parallel to the principal axis.

The two refracted rays intersect at the image of $A$, denoted by $A_1$;
other object points can be imaged in the same way.
The image is not formed by only two or three rays: in this approximation, many rays from $A$ converge at $A_1$ after passing through the lens and together form that image point.

The ray through the optical center $O$, namely $AOA_1$, also reaches $A_1$.
To locate an image point, we may therefore choose any two independent rays from the three special kinds:
1) A ray through the optical center.

2) A ray incident parallel to the principal axis.
3) A ray passing through the focus before reaching the lens.

Now consider an object point on the principal axis.
The three convenient special rays then coincide with the principal axis and do not by themselves determine an intersection point.
Figure 180 therefore selects an arbitrary point $B$ on the lens and the ray $SB$ arriving there.
Draw through the optical center a secondary optical axis parallel to $SB$, denoted by $PQ$;
on the outgoing-light side of the lens, draw the focal plane through the image-side focus $F$, perpendicular to the principal axis, and let its intersection with the secondary axis be $C$.

In the paraxial model, the refracted ray $BC$ passes through $C$;
together with the axial ray, this gives two light paths from the object point $S$.
The source shown lies between the focus and the converging lens, so the refracted rays diverge and their backward extensions locate the virtual image of $S$ at $S_1$.
Backward extensions are construction lines, not paths along which the light actually propagates.
